name: Nasal breathing meta

lead: The nasal breathing meta is the habit of breathing through the nose instead of the mouth, with the goal of a stronger jaw and midface, a better profile and a less bloated face. It is closely tied to mewing, mouth taping and discussions of nasal surgery.

Proponents say breathing pattern and tongue posture influence the growing jaw and midface. Research links chronic mouth breathing in children to facial growth patterns, sometimes called long face syndrome, and a systematic review and meta-analysis examined its effect on facial skeletal development, though cause can run in either direction. Studies on adults who switch to nasal breathing are much thinner.

paras: Users make nose breathing a default during the day and exercise, add mouth tape at night, and pair it with mewing posture. People with blocked noses often look at the obstruction first, since nasal obstruction is a main cause of mouth breathing.

Breathing through the nose is normal physiology. Mouth taping is little researched and is described as risky for anyone with nasal blockage or sleep apnea. Nasal surgery such as turbinate reduction carries surgical risks, and some users raise empty nose syndrome.

chain: Claimed better jaw and midface development
angle.text: Users favour nasal breathing, sometimes with mouth taping, for a stronger jaw and midface and a leaner-looking face. Studies in children link mouth breathing to growth changes; whether switching as an adult changes appearance has not been tested.

lead: The nasal breathing meta is the looksmaxxing belief that habitually breathing through the nose, rather than the mouth, supports healthy facial development, jaw and midface structure, and appearance. It is closely associated with mewing, mouth taping and discussions of nasal surgery.

Medical literature does describe a relationship between chronic mouth breathing in children and facial growth patterns, sometimes called long face syndrome, though causation can run in either direction [1]. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined the effects of mouth breathing on facial skeletal development in children. Evidence on adults is much thinner, and no study that the wiki has located tests whether adopting nasal breathing in adulthood changes facial appearance.

paras: Nasal breathing filters, warms and humidifies air, and nasal breathing is described as producing nitric oxide [1]. Chronic mouth breathing is reported to arise in most cases as an adaptation to nasal congestion, particularly during sleep [1]. Linked conditions include sleep apnea, snoring and anterior open bite [1].

Concern about mouth breathing is old: the painter and writer George Catlin published a book in 1862, later retitled Shut Your Mouth and Save Your Life, urging nose breathing, and a 1903 school hygiene book described a child with the typical face of a mouth-breather [1].

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis assessed how mouth breathing affects facial skeletal development and malocclusion in children, pooling cephalometric measures such as jaw position, facial height and overjet. A 2010 study compared mouth breathing and nasal breathing in orthodontic patients' dentofacial and craniofacial development. A general reference notes that much of the evidence comes from textbooks, reviews and small studies, and that the health effects of mouth taping have been little researched [1]. The relationship may also run in reverse, with a long narrow face and narrow nasopharynx predisposing to nasal obstruction [1].

Functional rhinoplasty and septal or turbinate surgery are described in reviews as treatments for nasal obstruction. Palatal expansion is discussed in some communities as a way to enlarge the nasal airway; clinical trials have measured nasal airflow after expansion in late adolescents and young adults. External nasal strips such as Breathe Right have been studied for snoring in a polysomnographic trial.

On looksmax.org, users compare options such as maxillary expansion and turbinate reduction for nasal breathing problems. In one thread a user warns against turbinate reduction citing empty nose syndrome, while another replies that reduction is the treatment for blockage from enlarged turbinates and calls expansion procedures gimmicks. Another encyclopedia article describes nasal breathing as a recommended habit among mewing proponents, who claim it supports airway development, and describes mouth taping as risky without professional supervision [2].

lore.intro: Nasal breathing is treated in these communities as a foundation habit for facial development and airway, linked to mewing and sometimes to surgical options [2].
